reference_title: Drilled Shafts: Construction Procedures and Design Methods

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body: Lateral loading typically controls the diameter of drilled shafts for highway bridges and may also control embedded length for retaining walls, noise walls, and sign/light standard foundations. Both geotechnical and structural design are required; structural design covered in Chapter 12. For rigorous coverage of laterally loaded deep foundations see FHWA GEC 9 (Parkes et al., 2018). This chapter does not explicitly address seismic design, but the methods can be used to determine linear or nonlinear spring constants for bases of structural columns for dynamic analysis.
key_points: Lateral loading typically controls shaft diameter; may control embedded length for retaining walls/sign structures
For detailed treatment see FHWA GEC 9 (Parkes et al., 2018)
Methods provide spring constants for structural dynamic analysis

sections.title: Examples of Lateral Loading Applications
sections.body: [pp. 9-1 to 9-9] Drilled shafts in highway projects mainly support bridge piers and abutments, but also retaining walls, overhead signs, sound walls and slope retention. Lateral loads come from earth pressures, centrifugal forces from vehicles, braking, wind, current, occasionally waves, ice, vessel impact and earthquakes (extreme events). Even without these, analysis may be needed for eccentric axial load and accidental batter. Monoshaft supports (one shaft per column) give a small footprint where geometry, access or other factors discourage multiple columns and groups, are increasingly used for aesthetics in tall structures, suit retrofit and widening, and are often more economical than multiple elements with a cap (Figure 9-1). Caltrans uses Type I and Type II designs (Figure 9-2): Type I has a continuous cage from shaft to column, the foundation being an extension of the column; Type II has a shaft at least 18 inches larger in diameter with a larger cage, so that any flexural overstress in an earthquake forms a plastic hinge at the column base / shaft top rather than at depth where inspection and repair are harder. Groups of shafts suit large lateral or vertical loads, multiple columns on one foundation, vessel impact, seismic, ice or wind on high bridges, and long unsupported lengths from scour, liquefaction or deep water; the common cap gives rotational restraint and turns column moments into axial shaft forces, the force couples giving rotational strength and stiffness. Figure 9-3 shows eight 7-ft shafts supporting two rectangular columns, similar to the I-35W Mississippi River replacement in Minneapolis, through scourable soil and about 40 ft into sandstone (groups in Chapter 11). Bridges over water take wind, current, waves, ship or barge impact, possibly seismic or ice loads, centrifugal and braking forces (sizeable for heavy trucks stopping on a downslope span), with scour lowering the ground; tall columns raise overturning, and a strut between columns can engage several shafts for vessel impact without a cap (Figure 9-4, Somerset, KY). Sound walls, signs and high mast lighting are lightly loaded vertically but carry significant transient, often cyclic, wind shear and overturning, sometimes vehicle impact: a two-shaft sign foundation (Figure 9-5a) resists the wind moment mainly by a push-pull couple with some bending for shear, a single shaft (Figure 9-5b) by bending; borings for such structures are often sparse, so designs must cover a range of conditions. In a survey of hurricane damage in Florida (Jones, 2005) the most common sign foundation failure was the anchor bolt connection at the shaft top, sometimes from poor concrete or misaligned bolts. Abutments carry backfill pressures (affected by settlement or creep), traffic surcharge, braking, thermal movement and seismic forces; large diameters let shafts take these without batter (Figure 9-6: (a) two rows of shafts resisting overturning by compression and tension; (b) a spill-through or stub abutment relying on the slope below; (c) tangent or secant shafts resisting load entirely in bending; examples, Figure 9-7). Arch bridges impose large thrusts on abutment shafts through thrust blocks (Figure 9-8). Retaining walls may be formed by secant or tangent shafts or shafts with clear spacing, tied back with ground anchors if cantilever action is insufficient (Figure 9-9), or shafts may support a conventional wall with soldier piles and precast panels (Figure 9-10). In slope stabilization (Figures 9-11, 9-12) forces from the moving mass transfer to the upper shaft, raising the factor of safety, and the shaft below the slip surface must resist them without excessive deflection or moment; drilling disturbs soil less than driving, crane rigs can reach 80 ft or more horizontally, and micropiles or anchors mainly mobilize axial resistance. Liquefaction-induced lateral spreading is a similar problem: the foundation either resists the movement or is loaded by passive pressure as the ground flows around it, and unless liquefaction is mitigated the foundation must be designed for this extreme event.

sections.title: Design Process
sections.body: [pp. 9-9 to 9-12] Lateral design can be controlled by geotechnical or structural strength or by serviceability. (1) Geotechnical strength limit state (resistance to overturning): the shaft must be large and deep enough to support the factored loads without collapse; deflections generally do not control, though a deflection causing collapse of other parts of the structure could be a strength limit; transient wind or extreme event cases are often most critical. (2) Structural strength limit state (flexure and shear): size and reinforcement must resist the bending, shear and axial loads. (3) Service limit state (deformations): lateral deformation and rotation under service loads must be tolerable at critical locations (typically the column top), and the shaft's translational and rotational stiffness must be determined for the structural analysis. Lateral design is Block 10 of the Chapter 8 process, subdivided in Figure 9-13. The subsurface data (Chapter 2) give a design profile for each lateral load case (Block 8, Figure 8-1; Block 10.1), allowing for variability of properties and strata elevations; sensitivity must be evaluated, and more than one design profile may be needed per location. Different load cases may need different profiles because of scour or liquefaction: design flood scour affects strength limit states, while check flood scour is an extreme event with different load and resistance factors (9.3.3.5). Routine design covers Blocks 10.2 to 10.6: the engineer must compute head deflection and rotation, the maximum moment and shear in the embedded shaft, and the nominal bending moment capacity (plastic hinge), which depends on the axial force; all depend largely on the soil or rock reaction and on the moment-rotation relation of the section, both nonlinear.
key_points: Geotechnical strength (overturning): support factored loads without collapse; often transient wind or extreme events
Structural strength: reinforcement and size for moment, shear and axial load
Service: deformation and rotation tolerable at the column top; provide stiffness to the structural analysis
Block 10 of the Chapter 8 process (Figure 9-13); a design profile per load case, more than one if variable

sections.title: Planning Stage Estimates
sections.body: [p. 9-12] Lateral load and flexural strength often control the minimum shaft diameter; for a single shaft under a single column these requirements are often reflected in the column size, and the preliminary shaft diameter is often set slightly larger than the column. The longitudinal reinforcement may be continuous with the column (despite greater cover in the shaft) or the shaft may use a larger cage for larger moments, e.g., long unsupported lengths at water crossings. A larger shaft diameter is usually desirable even if the reinforcement matches the column, so the cover can absorb the typical 3 to 6-inch construction location tolerance and still line the bars up with the column with the required minimum cover as built. Planning estimates of moment demand and resistance follow (9.3.2.1 to 9.3.2.3).
key_points: Flexure often controls minimum diameter; preliminary shaft slightly larger than the column
Cage continuous with the column or larger for long unsupported lengths

sections.title: Preliminary Estimate of Maximum Bending Moments (Demand)
sections.body: [pp. 9-12 to 9-14] To select a trial diameter and length (Block 10.2), a simple preliminary analysis estimates the maximum bending moment from estimated factored loads at the shaft top (from a frame analysis of the bridge, or simple statics for signs, lights and walls). The shaft below grade can be modeled as a free-standing column fixed at its base: the nonlinear beam on p-y springs (Figure 9-14a) is replaced by an equivalent cantilever (Figure 9-14b), and p-y analyses suggest the equivalent lengths of Figure 9-15 give a maximum moment about equal to a more sophisticated model. Figure 9-15 gives the equivalent fixity length in shaft diameters for estimating maximum moment below grade; the maximum moment generally does not occur at Lequiv, and there is really no such thing as a point of fixity. The values were computed for uniform clays from soft to hard (su of 3 to 50 psi) and medium to very dense sands (phi from 35 to 43 deg); very hard materials such as rock would have an equivalent length of less than one diameter. The chart estimates maximum moment only, for preliminary structural demand, and should not be used for displacement or rotation (example in 9.3.2.3).

sections.title: Estimating Nominal Bending Moment Resistance
sections.body: [p. 9-14] Structural design follows AASHTO 5.6.4 for reinforced concrete columns (Chapter 12), but for a trial diameter (Block 10.2) approximate nominal moment capacities can be used: (1) longitudinal reinforcing about 1% of the gross area, Mn (k-ft) ~ 27 D^3 (Eq. 9-1); (2) about 1.5%, Mn (k-ft) ~ 40 D^3 (Eq. 9-2), where D is the shaft diameter in ft and Mn the nominal moment resistance of a circular reinforced column with 3 inches cover and no axial compression. Axial compression generally increases Mn for tension-controlled members, so these are likely conservative. Structural design requires Mmax <= phi Mn, with phi for combined axial and bending (AASHTO 5.5.4.2) from 0.75 to 0.9, 0.9 typically governing where flexure dominates (Chapter 12).

sections.title: Example of Preliminary Analysis for Lateral Loading
sections.body: [pp. 9-14 to 9-15] Example: a column foundation with a factored ground-line shear of 40 kips and factored overturning moment of 800 kip-ft, a single shaft in very stiff clay with su estimated at 15 psi. For a 4-ft trial shaft (Step 10.2), Figure 9-15 suggests an equivalent fixity length of 1.5 to 1.7 diameters, 6.0 to 6.8 ft, so the maximum moment is about 800 k-ft + (6.8 ft)(40 k) = 1072 k-ft. A 4-ft shaft with 1% reinforcing has a factored moment capacity of at least (0.9)(27)(4)^3 = 1555 k-ft, well above 1072 k-ft (Step 10.4). Taking 1072 k-ft as the required factored capacity, the minimum diameter is D = {1072/[(0.9)(27)]}^(1/3) = 3.53 ft, so a 3.5 to 4 ft shaft is likely sufficient for complete design.

sections.title: Computational Procedures and Design Methodology (p-y Method)
sections.body: [p. 9-15] To complete design in Blocks 10.3 to 10.5 the engineer must (a) compute geotechnical resistance to overturning (Block 10.3), (b) compute the maximum moment and shear in the embedded shaft (Block 10.4), (c) compute the nominal moment capacity (Block 10.4), and (d) compute head deflection and rotation (Block 10.5), all influenced by the soil or rock reaction. The recommended method is the p-y method, modeling the shaft as a nonlinear elastic beam on nonlinear soil springs; it captures the essential mechanisms, has a history of successful use in transportation and offshore foundations, and needs a computer, with several user-friendly codes available (9.3.3.1).
key_points: Steps: overturning resistance, maximum moment and shear, nominal moment capacity, head deflection and rotation
Recommended: the p-y method (nonlinear beam on nonlinear springs), run by computer
sections.applicability: Final design lateral analysis; AASHTO strength and service limit state checks

sections.title: Brief Description of the p-y Method
sections.body: [pp. 9-15 to 9-17] The p-y method is the recommended, relatively sophisticated method capturing the nonlinear aspects; details are in GEC-9 (Parkes et al., 2018). It analyzes piles and shafts under combined axial and lateral loads, including distributed loads from flowing water or creeping soil, nonlinear bending with cracked sections, layered soils and/or rock and nonlinear soil response. Lateral load causes deflection and an opposing soil reaction that is a nonlinear function of deflection; the soil is modeled as nonlinear springs whose resistance p develops with deflection y (p-y curves). In the physical model (Figure 9-16) the soil reaction p at depth x (force per unit length) depends on deflection and on soil shear strength, Young's modulus, piezometric surface, shaft diameter, depth and whether loading is static (monotonic) or cyclic. p-y curves for static and cyclic loading come from full-scale experiments and theory (FHWA-RD-85-106, Reese, 1986), programmed as subroutines so the user inputs loads, section geometry and stiffness and soil, steel and concrete properties; other criteria (e.g., Murchison and O'Neill, 1984, the API method for sands; Reese, 1997, rock) and site-specific curves from load tests can be used. Cyclic criteria are important for wave, wind and seismic loading. Section 9.3.3.4 provides general design guidelines using currently available p-y models, and Section 9.3.3.5 is cited (as printed) for selection of the appropriate p-y model. The programs allow quick parametric study of loading, geometry, stiffness, penetration, soil properties and shaft-superstructure interaction, and buckling of a shaft extending above ground. A key use is varying penetration: head deflection varies considerably with penetration for short and intermediate shafts but not once the shaft is long. A tieback or strut can be simulated by a very stiff p-y curve at its location, and p-y curves can be offset by a specified displacement to simulate active pressure (9.3.6).

sections.body: [p. 9-17] Simulation of nonlinear bending in drilled shafts: 9.3.3.2.1 General and 9.3.3.2.2 Computation of Nonlinear Bending Stiffness.

sections.title: General
sections.body: [p. 9-17] A drilled shaft is a reinforced concrete beam-column whose bending cannot always be represented by a single EI. To find moments and shears for designing the steel and diameter, a linear analysis will almost always suffice; to estimate head deflections and rotations, nonlinear bending should be considered. Reinforcement must satisfy the moment demand for the structural limit state (Chapter 12). Moments from unavoidable axial load eccentricity dissipate within the top few diameters, even in weak surface soils; cages should be designed from moment and shear diagrams under the critical factored load combination, including axial loads at the bounds of the eccentricity allowed by the construction specifications, which permits reducing longitudinal steel with depth; the p-y method suits this.
key_points: Linear EI is almost always sufficient for moments and shears; use nonlinear EI for head deflection and rotation
Eccentricity moments dissipate within the top few diameters
Design the cage from factored moment and shear diagrams including permitted eccentricity; steel can reduce with depth

sections.title: Computation of Nonlinear Bending Stiffness
sections.body: [pp. 9-17 to 9-21] Concepts: when bending tension exceeds the concrete tensile strength the section cracks and EI drops dramatically; compressive axial load superimposes uniform compression, so the cracking moment depends on axial load, and cracks are assumed closely spaced wherever net tension exceeds tensile strength. Stress-strain: nonlinear curves are used for steel and concrete; concrete crushes at an ultimate strain ec of approximately 0.003, the steel ultimate strain in tension and compression is taken as 0.0020 (as printed), and the concrete tensile strength fr = 7.5 sqrt(f'c) (psi), linear in tension up to that stress. Moment-curvature: with plane sections remaining plane (Reese et al., 1998), an axial load Px and moment M displace the neutral axis, with equilibrium b int(h2..h1) sigma dy = Px (Eq. 9-3) and b int(h2..h1) sigma y dy = M (Eq. 9-4), terms defined in Figure 9-17. Procedure for compressive axial load and moment: estimate a neutral axis position and choose a strain gradient phi_e (strain per unit length, constant whether elastic or inelastic), defining the strain everywhere; compute stresses from the stress-strain curves; integrate to get the axial load (Eq. 9-3) and move the neutral axis until it equals Px; compute the moment (Eq. 9-4) about a convenient point; then EI = M / phi_e, phi_e being the curvature. Repeating for different phi_e gives the M-EI relation for each Px (Figure 9-18: 4-ft shaft, 12 #11 bars, 3 inches cover, axial 0, 200 and 400 kips); compressive axial load stiffens the section by delaying cracking, and here EI at the nominal moment is also higher. Current software typically uses the concrete model of Figure 9-19: f''c = 0.85 f'c (Eq. 9-5); Ec (initial slope) = 57,500 sqrt(f'c) (Eq. 9-6); fc = f''c [2(e/eo) - (e/eo)^2] for e < eo (Eq. 9-7); eo = 1.7 f'c / Ec (Eq. 9-8); fr = 7.5 sqrt(f'c) (Eq. 9-9), with Ec, fc, f'c and fr in psi and strain dimensionless (the figure shows stress falling by 0.15 f'c to a strain of .0038). Steel (Figure 9-20): ey = fy / E (Eq. 9-10) and E = 29,000,000 psi (Eq. 9-11), elastic-perfectly plastic in tension and compression. p-y software performs these computations automatically, adjusting EI along the shaft from relations like Figure 9-18; the user inputs concrete and steel strengths and section and bar geometry, and computed deflections, shears and moments then include cracking.

sections.title: Design of an Individual Drilled Shaft for Lateral Loading
sections.body: [p. 9-21] A shaft is designed for lateral loading to satisfy stability (geotechnical limit state), flexural strength (structural limit state) and deformations (service limit state), with diameter, penetration and reinforcement also considering axial loading and possibly other conditions (9.3.3.3.1 to 9.3.3.3.4).
key_points: Check geotechnical, structural and service limit states, together with axial design
sections.applicability: Limit state design of a single laterally loaded drilled shaft

sections.title: Geotechnical Strength Limit State
sections.body: [pp. 9-21 to 9-23] The shaft must be large and deep enough to support the factored loads for each load case without collapse; deflections do not control. p-y procedure for a trial diameter and penetration: (1) model the shaft as a linear elastic beam with E of concrete (about 4,000,000 psi) and the uncracked I = pi D^4/64, so convergence is not limited by flexural strength (checked later); (2) model the soil with the best estimate of governing conditions for each load case, using the least favorable conditions within the zone a model represents, separate models for significant variations (Block 10.1), and local scour where required; (3) apply the head load in multiples up to and beyond the factored load as a pushover analysis (Block 10.3), instability showing as non-convergence or an extremely large deflection; (4) the computed deflection must be reasonable, 10% of the shaft diameter, at and slightly above the factored load; (5) reserve strength above the factored load ensures ductility and covers site variability, provided by a resistance factor below one. AASHTO Table 10.5.5.2.4-1 (2017) gives 1.0 for nominal horizontal geotechnical resistance of a single shaft or group and for extreme limit states, but Table 9-1 values are recommended: overturning of an individual or single row of elastic shafts free to rotate at the head, 0.67; pushover of an elastic shaft in a multiple row group with moment connection to the cap, 0.8; extreme event strength cases, 0.8. These are the authors' suggested values, a ductility and stability check exceeding the reliability of current AASHTO (2017a) provisions. The pushover model should converge at loads at least 1/phi times the factored load for each strength case, with deflections no larger than 10% of the diameter; the column, connection or shaft may not actually be strong enough to carry 1/phi times the load, but the elastic-beam analysis only ensures adequate embedment for strength and ductility from soil resistance. Trial diameters and lengths can be run quickly to find a minimum; if the diameter is set by other factors (column size, anchor bolt pattern) the minimum embedment for lateral load is found for it; axial or other design may require more.

sections.title: Structural Strength Limit State
sections.body: [p. 9-23] The shaft must be large enough and reinforced longitudinally and transversely so its nominal axial, shear and flexural resistance exceed the factored effects. At Block 10.4 only a preliminary structural check is made; final structural design, with the connection to the structure, is Block 12 of Figure 8-1, and lateral loads are likely to control it. The linear elastic geotechnical analyses give moments at the factored loads; the maximum moment depends on loads and soil resistance, and nonlinear EI (9.3.3.2.2) has relatively little effect on it. A quick check uses the preliminary resistance of 9.3.2.2: if computed moments greatly exceed the estimate for about 1.5% reinforcing, consider a larger diameter. Complete structural design (Chapter 12): factored axial, shear and moment; longitudinal steel giving nominal strength above the combined factored axial force and moment for each combination; and concrete shear resistance compared with factored shear, adding transverse steel beyond the code minimum if needed.
key_points: Preliminary structural check at Block 10.4; final design in Block 12 (Chapter 12)
Maximum moment is insensitive to nonlinear EI
If moments greatly exceed Mn at about 1.5% steel (Eq. 9-2), enlarge the shaft
Longitudinal steel for combined axial and moment; transverse steel for shear beyond the minimum

sections.title: Serviceability Limit State (Lateral Deformations)
sections.body: [p. 9-24] Deformation limits should come from the structure's actual serviceability requirements, not rules of thumb. Head deformation and rotation of a single column, single shaft can be amplified at the pier cap of a tower bent. Signs and sound walls are not very sensitive to deformation, though limits may be set for aesthetics or function, and some extreme event cases (e.g., check flood scour, some seismic loads) may have no serviceability requirement. Much of the deformation may come from the shaft's flexural stiffness rather than the ground, so the nonlinear section model (9.3.3.2.2) should be used with service loads; this needs only the service loads and the nonlinear material input (longitudinal steel, concrete strength and modulus) added to the strength model.
key_points: Use the structure's actual serviceability limits, not rules of thumb
Head movement may amplify at the top of a tall bent; signs and walls are less sensitive
Use nonlinear EI with service loads: flexural cracking can dominate deformation

sections.title: Example
sections.body: [pp. 9-24 to 9-28] Example continuing 9.3.2.3: factored loads 40 kips shear and 800 kip-ft moment at the ground line; very stiff clay with su = 15 psi; 4-ft trial shaft; maximum service loads 25 kips shear plus 500 kip-ft; service head deflection not to exceed 1/2 inch (Figure 9-21). Geotechnical strength: LPILE p-y analyses of the 4-ft shaft with loads in proportion to the factored loads and several embedded lengths, inputs being head shear and moment (axial 0), diameter 48 inches with E = 4,000,000 psi and I = pi d^4/64 = 260,576 in^4, the length in 100 nodes, and clay with unit weight 0.07 pci, cohesion 15 psi and default e50 = 0.005. With phi = 0.67 (Table 9-1), the elastic shaft must converge with deflection not exceeding 10% of the diameter (4.8 inches) at 1.5 (1/0.67) times the factored loads, 60 kips shear + 1200 kip-ft (Figure 9-22a). A 15 ft shaft is marginal, its deflection at that load exceeding 4.8 inches; 5 ft more embedment gives a much more robust design. The maximum moment hardly depends on length (Figure 9-22b): about 880 kip-ft at the factored load for 20 and 25-ft shafts (873 and 885), somewhat less than the 1072 k-ft preliminary estimate; the 20-ft by 4-ft shaft is carried forward. Structural and service: nonlinear 48-inch section with 12 #11 bars (about 1% steel) at 3 inches cover, f'c 4,500 psi, fy 60,000 psi (Figure 9-23). The maximum factored moment is 865 k-ft against 873 k-ft for the linear model, confirming insensitivity to EI. Service head deflection is 0.13 inches under 25 kips and 500 k-ft, well within 0.5 inch, compared with 0.07 inches for the linear EI, the difference coming mainly from cracking. Moment-curvature and moment-EI (Figures 9-24, 9-25) give a nominal moment (Mult) of 1791 k-ft, well above the factored demand. The example covers geotechnical strength (diameter and length), structural strength (diameter and steel) and service deflection; full design must consider all other loads, especially axial, and possibly groups (Chapter 11).

sections.title: Guidelines for Selection of Appropriate p-y Criteria for Design
sections.body: [p. 9-28] An overview of available p-y criteria with guidance on their selection for typical transportation design; fuller descriptions are in the cited references and software manuals. p-y criteria associate mobilized soil resistance with displacement along the shaft; although some have a theoretical basis, the criteria used in design are empirical, derived from instrumented load tests, so users must understand each criterion's experimental basis and limitations.
key_points: p-y criteria are empirical, from instrumented load tests: know each one's basis and limits
sections.applicability: Choosing p-y criteria for lateral analysis of drilled shafts

sections.title: Cohesive Soils
sections.body: [pp. 9-28 to 9-30] Common criteria for cohesive soils are soft clay (Matlock, 1970), stiff clay (Welch and Reese, 1972) and stiff clay in the presence of free water (Reese et al., 1975), each a polynomial resistance-displacement curve with an upper bound (Figure 9-26). The most influential input is the undrained shear strength su, which directly affects the ultimate resistance Pu, typically from UU triaxial tests at confining pressures at or near the total overburden pressure. Less influential is the initial stiffness Esi, commonly related to e50, the strain at 50% of the yield stress in the UU test, often simply associated with a range of su. su correlates reliably with short-duration load tests (a few hours), appropriate for highway live loads; sustained loads may mobilize a softer response (creep) and very short transient loads a stiffer one (rate effects). Analyses should use a range of su and e50 to test sensitivity. The Reese et al. (1975) stiff clay with free water criterion came from cyclic tests in submerged stiff fissured clay (su about 2 ksf) whose response degraded rapidly from local scour beside the pile, and its static curve also strain-softens (Figure 9-27), giving much less resistance than Welch and Reese (1972); it is appropriate only where stiff clay is exposed to free water at or near the surface (e.g., water crossings). Where groundwater is at depth and no free water is at the surface, Welch and Reese is more appropriate, even below groundwater, and stiff clay below a sand stratum would normally not degrade unless scour removed the sand.
key_points: Soft clay (Matlock, 1970), stiff clay (Welch and Reese, 1972), stiff clay with free water (Reese et al., 1975)
su (UU triaxial at about overburden pressure) governs Pu; e50 sets the less influential initial stiffness
Calibrated on short-duration tests: creep softens sustained loads, rate stiffens transient loads
Run a range of su and e50
Use the free-water stiff clay criterion only where stiff clay is exposed to free water at the surface; otherwise Welch and Reese

sections.title: Cohesionless Soils (Sands)
sections.body: [p. 9-30] Common criteria for cohesionless soils are Cox et al. (1974) and the very similar Murchison and O'Neill (1984) criterion adopted as a standard by the American Petroleum Institute, each an initial linear stiffness followed by a polynomial transition to an upper bound (Figure 9-28). The most influential input is the modulus k, setting the initial straight line, estimated within 20 to 225 lb/in.^3 from the relative density and whether the sand is submerged or dry. The ultimate resistance Pu depends on phi and confining pressure, but the lateral response is less sensitive to phi than to k.
key_points: Cox et al. (1974) or the API criterion (Murchison and O'Neill, 1984)
Modulus k, 20 to 225 lb/in.^3 by relative density and submergence, governs response
Response less sensitive to phi than to k

sections.title: Cohesive Granular (c-phi) Soils
sections.body: [pp. 9-30 to 9-31] The c-phi criterion in some commercial software superposes the cohesive and cohesionless criteria; it is not supported by experimental data and not recommended for foundation design. Without site-specific load tests to calibrate an alternative, use either a cohesionless soil or a cohesive soil with a best estimate of undrained strength versus depth. Full scale tests in cemented granular soil (loess) in Kansas produced a loess p-y criterion (Johnson et al., 2007).
key_points: Superposed c-phi criterion: no experimental support, not recommended
Use sand or clay criteria (best-estimate su) unless load tests calibrate another

sections.title: Rock
sections.body: [pp. 9-31 to 9-32] Rock p-y methods rest on limited experiments and correlations (Reese, 1997); the weak rock recommendations are conservative for most design. The weak rock curve (Figure 9-29) resembles the cohesive one with ultimate resistance from compressive strength qu rather than su, and krm in place of e50; the initial stiffness Kir is proportional to qu, the initial rock mass modulus Eir and krm, with krm suggested from 0.00005 to 0.0005 (the lower value stiffer). In tests of 3 to 5-ft shafts embedded 1 to 2 diameters in severely weathered, decomposed quartzite (SPT 50 blows for less than 2 inches, recovery under 20%, RQD 0; Brown and Kahle, 2002), loaded to overturning failure, the weak rock criterion with qu = 180 psi, Eir = 27,000 psi (150 qu) and krm = 0.0004 modeled the results very effectively, a reasonable lower bound for hard but decomposed rock when the investigation gives little strength information. Strong rock uses a bilinear model from vuggy limestone in southern Florida (Figure 9-30, Ensoft, Inc., 2004), with su = 1/2 qu and b the shaft diameter. Because the tests reached only limited displacement, brittle fracture was assumed at a displacement of 0.24% of the diameter (about 0.1 inches for a 3.5-ft shaft, 0.2 inches for 7-ft), beyond which resistance drops to zero, so the strong rock criterion can curiously give a weaker response than weak rock with similar strengths. Such brittle behavior is unlikely for most rock; use the weak rock criterion where shear failure of the rock mass is considered possible.
key_points: Weak rock (Reese, 1997): Pu from qu, krm 0.00005 to 0.0005; conservative for most design
Decomposed quartzite tests (Brown and Kahle, 2002): qu = 180 psi, Eir = 27,000 psi (150 qu), krm = 0.0004 as a lower bound
Strong rock (vuggy limestone, Ensoft 2004): bilinear, brittle at 0.24% of the diameter, then zero
Strong rock can compute weaker than weak rock; use weak rock where rock mass shear failure is possible

sections.title: Correlations with In-Situ Tests
sections.body: [p. 9-32] Published correlations compute p-y curves from in-situ tests such as the pressuremeter (Briaud, 1992) or dilatometer (Robertson et al., 1985), empirically considering soil type, depth and diameter. Comparative evaluations suggest useful correlations (Anderson et al., 2003); calibration to field load tests in representative local geology gives the most reliable use.
key_points: Pressuremeter (Briaud, 1992) and dilatometer (Robertson et al., 1985) p-y correlations
Calibrate to local load tests
sections.applicability: Deriving p-y curves from pressuremeter or dilatometer tests

sections.title: Variations in Stratigraphy
sections.body: [p. 9-33] Variations in stratigraphy are often more significant than the strength of any one stratum, particularly a soft layer over rock. Example (Figure 9-31): a 6-ft by 40-ft shaft through 20 ft of soft clay (su = 2 psi) into weak rock (qu = 180 psi, Erm = 27,000 psi) under 75 kips shear at the surface. Base case: deflection 0.116 in., maximum moment 15,722 in.-kip. Soft clay 10% thicker: 0.142 (+22%), 16,590 (+5.5%). Soft clay strength 10% lower: 0.118 (+2%), 15,880 (+1%). Rock qu and Erm 10% lower: 0.118 (+2%), 15,720 (no change). Strong rock bearing, qu = 750 psi: 0.125 (+8%), 15,410 (-2%). Defining stratigraphy and its possible variation matters most, and sensitivity analysis shows the key parameters. The strong rock (vuggy limestone) criterion gave a larger displacement even at qu = 750 psi than weak rock at 180 psi, suggesting limits on its use beyond the formation it came from.
key_points: Stratigraphy often matters more than strength of one layer
Example 6-ft x 40-ft shaft, 20 ft soft clay over weak rock, 75 kips: base 0.116 in., 15,722 in.-kip
Clay 10% thicker: +22% deflection; strength changes of 10%: about +2%

sections.title: Effects of Cyclic Loading
sections.body: [p. 9-33] Repeated cyclic lateral loading can reduce soil resistance (most in cohesive soils), and the p-y criteria include a degradation model. The largest effect is in submerged conditions where large surface displacements open a gap: water is sucked in and expelled with each cycle, eroding the soil and enlarging the gap, a significant concern for coastal structures under repeated waves.
key_points: Cyclic degradation strongest in submerged clays with gapping and erosion
Important for coastal structures under repeated waves
sections.applicability: Accounting for cyclic lateral loading in p-y analysis

sections.title: Effects of Rate of Loading
sections.body: [p. 9-34] Short transient loads (seismic, wind, vessel impact) load the soil faster than static load tests run over hours, on which the p-y criteria are based; higher strain rates generally give a somewhat stiffer, stronger response, so static analyses may be somewhat conservative, but direct rate effects are generally not justified for routine design. Long-term sustained loads (e.g., earth pressure) may have the opposite effect, creep in clays reducing stiffness relative to short-term curves based on undrained strength.
key_points: Fast transient loads: stiffer and stronger; static analysis somewhat conservative; no rate adjustment routinely
Sustained loads in clay: creep softens the response
sections.applicability: Rate-of-loading effects on lateral soil resistance

sections.title: Considerations for Scour and Extreme Event Loading
sections.body: [p. 9-34] Extreme event combinations may include earthquakes, ice, vessel impact and check flood scour; the 100 year flood scour is not an extreme event but needs special consideration, and some extreme events combine with different scour levels (e.g., vessel impact). Recurrence intervals of extreme events are thought to exceed the design life. Ice and vessel impact use the static procedures with various scour combinations. Scour lowers the surface of the Block 10.1 profiles and includes general scour, contraction scour and local pier scour (Chapter 10). Design flood effects are included at strength and service limit states; check flood scour is an extreme condition that may lower the surface more for strength combinations, and AASHTO 10.5.5.3.2 requires the nominal resistance remaining after the check flood to support the unfactored strength limit state loads with a resistance factor of 1.00. Earthquake loads from the structure are typically analyzed by the static procedures with additional considerations (9.4).
key_points: Extreme events: earthquake, ice, vessel impact, check flood scour; 100 year flood scour is not extreme
Scour = general + contraction + local; lowers the design profile
After check flood scour, nominal resistance must carry unfactored strength loads with phi = 1.00 (AASHTO 10.5.5.3.2)

sections.title: Alternative Models for Computation of Shaft Response
sections.body: [p. 9-35] Although the p-y method is recommended, alternatives can be used in some circumstances. The Broms Method (Broms, 1964a, 1964b, 1965) is a simple computation that may be useful for sign or sound wall foundations on short shafts, and a rational limit equilibrium solution easy to understand for the strength limits of a simple problem. Other alternatives are elastic continuum, boundary element and finite element models (overview in GEC-9, Parkes et al., 2018).
key_points: p-y method recommended
Broms Method: simple limit equilibrium, useful for short sign or sound wall shafts
Elastic continuum, boundary and finite element models (GEC-9)

sections.title: Design of Drilled Shaft Walls
sections.body: [p. 9-35] Drilled shaft walls may be secant, tangent or soldier pile (shaft) walls (Figure 9-32). Soldier pile walls have spaces between shafts with or without lagging or panels; closely spaced shafts let soil arch between them, covered with panels or shotcrete for finish and erosion protection. Secant walls combine unreinforced primary shafts, sometimes of lower strength concrete, with reinforced secondary shafts built soon after. Tangent walls are used where groundwater is less of a concern, since the joints are not sealed. All types can take a curtain wall or facing and drainage between facing and joints, or gravel columns behind joints with horizontal relief holes; examples were shown in Section 9.2.5 (as printed). Shaft walls suit cuts needing a wall built in advance; soldier pile walls can have steel sections and panels above the shaft top to retain backfill; secant and tangent reinforcement can be cages or structural steel; walls can carry vertical loads as well as earth and water pressure. Chapter 9 of GEC-9 gives a simple approach for single-row shaft walls, AASHTO Section 11.8 (nongravity cantilevered walls) applies, and shaft footings for gravity or semi-gravity walls follow Section 9.3.

Facing, drainage layers or gravel columns with relief holes

sections.title: Design for Drilled Shaft Foundations with Lateral Movement of Soil Mass
sections.body: [pp. 9-36 to 9-37] Shafts may be loaded by a moving soil mass (slope instability, liquefaction-induced lateral spreading) or used to restrain it as a slope remedy; the unstable mass can impose up to passive pressure, so shafts must be embedded below it for geotechnical strength and be structurally strong enough. Pressures above the slip surface give shear and overturning at the slip surface, and the shaft below is analyzed by the earlier methods (group effects per Chapter 11). A structure in an unstable slope would normally include remedial stability measures, but liquefaction-induced spreading may be designed for; it may give low passive pressure in the liquefied zone, but an intact overlying mass can add significant pressure. A lesser restraining force than passive may prevent full slope failure: limit equilibrium analysis (Modified Bishop, Simplified Janbu or Spencer) with a horizontal restraining force gives the required force, the design force above the slip surface being the lesser of passive pressure and the force needed for overall stability. AASHTO (2017a) 11.6.2.3 requires overall stability with a resistance factor of 0.65 where the slope contains or supports a structural element. Alternatively, p-y curves above the slip plane can be offset by a displacement, giving shaft shear and moment versus soil movement, useful for deep slip planes where shafts act as shear dowels. Figure 9-33 (Loehr and Brown, 2007): clay over rock with the slip at the interface, offsets up to 3 inches tapering to 0 over an 18-inch shear zone, with nonlinear p-y and moment-curvature; shear and moment grow with soil movement. This evaluates the socket's geotechnical strength below the shear plane, overall slope stability with the shaft force as restraint, the shaft's structural strength, and (approximately) slope deformation versus restraining force. The p-y criteria are short-term, so creep in clay may relax pressures or add movement, but shaft shear and moment are not very sensitive to the p-y response for a deep failure surface (details in Loehr and Brown, 2007, and GEC-9). Liquefaction-induced instability is discussed in 9.4.
key_points: Moving soil can load shafts up to passive pressure; embed below the slip surface and design structurally
Design force = lesser of passive pressure and the restraint needed for overall stability (limit equilibrium)
AASHTO 11.6.2.3: overall stability resistance factor 0.65 where the slope contains or supports a structure

sections.title: Design for Seismic Loading
sections.body: [p. 9-38] Seismic response of bridges is complex and nonlinear: ground motion reaches the superstructure through kinematic interaction with the foundations, possibly differing from free-field motion, and the accelerated superstructure mass generates inertial forces that return through the foundations, so soil-foundation interaction plays a key role. A rigorous direct method analyzing ground and structure together is impractical for most bridges, though warranted for some large nonconventional ones; routine design uses the substructure method, analyzing free-field ground response, foundation response and structure response separately and iterating for compatibility. Key components: (1) free-field ground response (response spectrum or acceleration time series); (2) structural analysis of component demands, including foundations; (3) foundation analysis supporting the structural analysis and foundation design for strength and deformation. Seismic demand depends on proximity to sources, regional and local ground conditions and return period, typically by probabilistic seismic hazard analysis from mapped spectral accelerations or site-specific studies, not covered here (AASHTO, 2017a; FHWA-NHI-15-004, Marsh et al., 2014). Foundation designers are responsible for item 3 and support item 2: they provide foundation stiffness as equivalent springs and inform the structural designer of demands from permanent seismic ground deformation, in an iterative, communicative process. Subsections: 9.4.1 framework; 9.4.2 excess pore pressure and liquefaction; 9.4.3 cyclic softening of cohesive soils; 9.4.4 foundation stiffness, damping and input motions.
key_points: Kinematic and inertial interaction make soil-foundation interaction central
Routine bridges: substructure method (ground, foundation, structure solved separately and iterated)

sections.title: Framework for Structural Analysis of Earthquake Effects
sections.body: [pp. 9-39 to 9-40] The manual follows AASHTO LRFD (2017a), which uses the force-based method (FBM); the displacement-based method (DBM) is in the AASHTO Guide Specifications for LRFD Seismic Bridge Design (2015). Foundation design is much the same either way. Both aim to prevent collapse, with plastic hinges in above-ground columns or piers yielding in a controlled, ductile way as fuses that limit forces on foundations and connections, since column damage can be assessed and repaired but foundation damage is hard to detect and repair (the motive for Caltrans Type II, Figure 9-2). Demand for conventional bridges is usually computed by elastic methods: equivalent-static methods from an acceleration (FBM) or displacement (DBM) response spectrum at the fundamental period (single or multi-modal; the most common approach), or elastic response history analysis; nonlinear pushover or response history methods, mostly with DBM, are informative but expensive, expert and still uncertain (Marsh et al., 2014). In FBM, elastic forces in yielding elements are reduced by an R-factor to their plastic capacity, and the remaining capacity-protected elements are designed to stay elastic. Drilled shafts are typically capacity-protected and designed elastic: R = 1.0 is required by AASHTO (2017a) 3.10.9.4 in Seismic Zones 3 or 4 and recommended for critical or essential bridges in Zone 2; for ordinary Zone 2 bridges, 3.10.9.3 permits one-half the R-factor of the supported substructure component but not less than 1.0. Shafts need not be designed for more than the forces from column plastic hinging with material overstrength if those are less than the elastic demand. In DBM, displacement demands are compared with displacement capacity (ductility factor mu, minimum values in the Guide Specifications, 2015), other components being capacity-protected. FBM achieves ductility by prescriptive detailing, so its deformations are more uncertain, and nonconventional (e.g., cable-stayed) and lifeline structures often use DBM, which also suits higher performance criteria. Some owners permit below-ground hinging and limited shaft inelasticity, usually with DBM, for extended pile-shafts or lateral spreading where preventing it is too costly. The foundation designer should confirm with the structural designer whether FBM or DBM is used (which AASHTO document applies) and whether below-ground hinging is allowed. The structural designer determines the factored shear, moment and axial demands on the shafts; the p-y method suits the seismic analysis, accounting for excess pore pressure, liquefaction or cyclic softening and permanent lateral ground displacement (9.4.2, 9.4.3).

sections.title: Effects of Excess Pore Water Pressure Generation including Liquefaction
sections.body: [p. 9-41] In saturated loose cohesionless soils, cyclic shear strain during shaking generates excess pore pressure and reduces effective stress, reducing lateral resistance (Extreme Event I limit state) and axial side resistance (10.7). The excess pore pressure is expressed as the ratio ru = Delta u / sigma'v0 (Eq. 9-12); as ru approaches 1 effective stress is essentially zero and liquefaction occurs, which can drastically reduce lateral and axial resistance and cause lateral spreading; significant excess pore pressure without liquefaction should also be considered. Idriss and Boulanger (2008) give a three-part framework of susceptibility, triggering and consequences (also Kavazanjian et al., 2011; Marsh et al., 2014).
key_points: Excess pore pressure reduces lateral and axial resistance (Extreme Event I)
ru = Delta u / sigma'v0 (Eq. 9-12); liquefaction as ru approaches 1
Evaluate susceptibility, triggering and consequences (Idriss and Boulanger, 2008)
equations: Eq. 9-12: r_u = Delta u / sigma'_v0 - excess pore water pressure ratio (pre-earthquake vertical effective stress)
sections.applicability: Excess pore pressure and liquefaction effects on drilled shafts

sections.title: Susceptibility
sections.body: [p. 9-41] Most susceptible are loose, non-plastic or low-plasticity, recently deposited cohesionless sediments, natural or man-made, especially hydraulic fills; this generally excludes cohesive soils and granular soils with moderate to high fines, particularly plastic fines. Susceptibility is assessed from grain size, Atterberg limits and/or the CPT soil behavior type index Ic (Idriss and Boulanger, 2008), always before triggering analysis, and non-susceptible layers are excluded, since triggering methods may otherwise predict liquefaction in them misleadingly.
key_points: Loose, non-plastic, young cohesionless soils and hydraulic fills are most susceptible
Screen by gradation, Atterberg limits or CPT Ic before triggering; exclude non-susceptible layers
sections.applicability: Screening soils for liquefaction susceptibility

sections.title: Triggering
sections.body: [pp. 9-41 to 9-42] Triggering is the onset of liquefaction, ru = 1.0, usually assessed by the simplified method (Seed and Idriss, 1971): demand as maximum cyclic shear stress and resistance from CPT or SPT penetration, normalized as CSR and CRR, with FSliq = CRR/CSR. CPT methods are generally preferred for their continuous profile in interbedded alluvium and easy import into software. The empirical relations come from case histories, are updated frequently (including Canterbury 2010-2011 and Tohoku 2011 since the 2010 manual, informing fines content, duration and large magnitude effects), and users should check each method's basis and limits. The FSliq profile delineates liquefying layers (FSliq <= 1.0), layers that may generate significant excess pore pressure (1.0 < FSliq <~ 1.5) and layers not susceptible to strength loss, plus layers susceptible to cyclic softening; do this early so trial designs embed below liquefiable layers.
key_points: Simplified method (Seed and Idriss, 1971): FSliq = CRR/CSR; CPT generally preferred
FSliq <= 1.0 liquefies; 1.0 to about 1.5 significant excess pore pressure; also flag cyclic softening
Evaluate early so shafts embed below liquefiable layers
sections.applicability: Liquefaction triggering evaluation for drilled shaft design

sections.title: Consequences
sections.body: [pp. 9-42 to 9-45] FSliq with penetration resistance and index properties gives the consequence parameters: residual undrained strength su,r, maximum cyclic shear strain gamma_max and ru (for 1.0 < FSliq <~ 1.5), generated automatically by common software. The main consequence for shafts is reduced axial and lateral stiffness and strength; reduced lateral stiffness often drives maximum flexural demand deeper and larger and changes the superstructure's dynamic response (axial in 10.7, groups in Chapter 11). Consequences scale with severity (e.g., FSliq) and depend on layer thickness, depth and continuity, slope and its gradient relative to the liquefied layer depth, shaking duration and the strata above and below; a thin marginal layer under thick nonliquefiable soil likely matters little, and medium dense and dense soils may trigger (ru = 1.0) but develop limited shear strain (Figure 9-34; Ishihara and Yoshimine, 1992; Idriss and Boulanger, 2008; Cetin et al., 2009). Consequences should therefore be quantified from strength loss (ru, su,r) or deformation (gamma_max) parameters, not a binary liquefaction criterion. Residual strength from SPT by Kramer and Wang (2015) (Figure 9-35): su,r = exp(-8.444 + 0.109[(N1)60] + 5.379(sigma'v0)^0.1) >= drained strength (Eq. 9-13), with (N1)60 the overburden- and energy-corrected SPT blow count and sigma'v0 and su,r in atmospheres; other SPT/CPT correlations are in Idriss and Boulanger (2008). gamma_max from FSliq and relative density follows Ishihara and Yoshimine (1992) as approximated by Idriss and Boulanger (2008) (Figure 9-34), limited to DR >= 40%, looser soils developing large strain immediately on triggering; SPT/CPT-based equivalents exist. For 1 < FSliq <~ 1.5, ru can be estimated from the Marcuson et al. (1990) stress-based data by the hyperbolic fit ru = 1 / [1 + 15(FSliq - 1.0)] for FSliq > 1 (Eq. 9-14), or, since shear strain relates more closely to pore pressure generation, from gamma_max by Cetin and Bilge (2012): ru = exp{ln[1 - exp(-(-0.407 gamma_max)/(-0.486 + 0.025 ln sigma'v0 - DR/100) x (0.620/(1 + gamma_max) + 1))]} (Eq. 9-15), gamma_max from Idriss and Boulanger (2008) or Figure 9-34.
key_points: Consequence parameters: su,r, gamma_max and ru; reduced stiffness drives moment deeper and larger

sections.title: Liquefied Soil in p-y Analyses
sections.body: [pp. 9-45 to 9-47] Liquefaction can enter p-y analyses by (1) a soft clay p-y model with pult = su,r (e.g., Wang and Reese, 1998), (2) a sand p-y model with a p-multiplier (e.g., Brandenberg et al., 2007), or (3) a curve formulated for liquefied sand (Franke and Rollins, 2013). For (1), Wang and Reese (1998) recommend e50 = 0.05 in the Matlock (1970) soft clay curve; Matlock's cyclic reduction option, for sensitive clays under many wind or wave cycles, is generally not applicable to seismic problems (Brandenberg et al., 2007). Figure 9-36 gives p-multipliers (Pm) for liquefaction from centrifuge studies (Brandenberg, 2005) and case history back-analyses (AIJ, 2001), typically about 0.05 to 0.25 for loose to medium-dense sands, giving a curve shaped like nonliquefied sand with reduced resistance and stiffness (Figure 9-37); group p-multipliers (Chapter 11) can be combined with them. Reduced unit weight is a similar approach: Brown and Camp (2002) matched a lateral test on an 8-ft shaft in blast-liquefied loose to medium dense silty sand using 15% of the soil unit weight, but this also lowers effective stress below, so use caution unless liquefaction is confined to thin surface layers. Blast tests by Rollins et al. (2005) under inertial (pile head) loading gave concave-up curves at large displacement from dilation; Kashighandi and Brandenberg (2010) and Ashford et al. (2011) advise against using the dilative response for kinematic lateral spreading in equivalent-static analysis, so a concave-down curve should represent liquefied soil for kinematic loading (concave-up curves can also cause convergence problems). Franke and Rollins (2013) proposed a hybrid taking the lesser of the Rollins et al. (2005) curve and the Matlock curve with pult from su,r, matching inertial and kinematic case histories well. Where lateral spreading displacement is significant, curve shape does not control and the nonliquefied crust, which imposes larger loads, matters much more. For 1 < FSliq <~ 1.5, resistance should drop with effective stress but the relation is not well understood; Chang and Hutchinson (2013) shake table tests with ru about 1% to 20% showed concave-up curves near the surface (ru about 10-20%) and static-like curves below (ru < 10%), and recommend scaling factors on the Rollins et al. curve for 0.1 < ru < 1.0 for inertial loading. Absent better research, p-multipliers can be interpolated between Pm,liq at ru = 100% (e.g., Figure 9-36) and the estimated ru (Eq. 9-14 or 9-15) after Dobry et al. (1995): Pm = 1 - ru(1 - Pm,liq) for 1 < FSliq <= 1.5 (Eq. 9-16). For FSliq >~ 1.5 no pore pressure degradation is needed, though curves may be adjusted for other dynamic effects.
key_points: Options: soft clay curve with pult = su,r (e50 = 0.05), sand curve with p-multiplier, or a liquefied-sand curve
Matlock cyclic reduction not for seismic problems
Liquefaction p-multipliers typically about 0.05 to 0.25 (Figure 9-36); combine with group multipliers
Reduced unit weight (15%, Brown and Camp, 2002) only for thin surface layers
Use concave-down curves for kinematic loading; Franke and Rollins (2013) hybrid
Large spreading: crust properties matter more than curve shape
Pm = 1 - ru(1 - Pm,liq) for 1 < FSliq <= 1.5 (Eq. 9-16, after Dobry et al., 1995)

sections.title: Liquefaction-Induced Lateral Spreading or Flow Failure
sections.body: [pp. 9-47 to 9-50] Where liquefied soil underlies a slope or is near a free face, static driving shear stress (tau_static) plus shaking inertia can accumulate downslope displacement of the liquefied soil and overlying crust: lateral spreading, where su,r exceeds tau_static and displacement occurs only with inertial forces, hence concurrently with them. Where su,r < tau_static the ground is statically unstable and a flow slide with displacements of tens or hundreds of feet results. Both can impose large kinematic loads, especially with a nonliquefied crust; a flow slide usually requires ground improvement, since the ground failure would make infrastructure unusable anyway. Design methods (Kavazanjian et al., 2011, from MCEER/ATC-49-1, 2003; Ashford et al., 2011) are equivalent-static: a free-field spreading displacement profile is imposed on the free ends of p-y springs, matching case histories well (Brandenberg et al., 2013; Ledezma and Gonzalez, 2014; Turner et al., 2016; Franke and Rollins, 2017). Nonlinear dynamic continuum analyses are uncertain and slow, unsuitable for routine design but possibly warranted to verify critical lifeline bridges. Components (Figure 9-38): define p-y springs for liquefied and nonliquefied layers; impose the spreading displacement profile; represent foundations and other resisting or affected substructure (columns, caps, column-to-deck connections); run the analysis. Free-field displacement predictions (Youd et al., 2002; Zhang et al., 2004; Faris et al., 2006) vary widely, but with several feet or more of displacement crust passive pressure is fully mobilized and shafts are insensitive to the exact value; design for low displacement only where several methods agree it is minimal, otherwise for fully mobilized crust loads, and do not apply the methods outside their empirical range (deep or distant liquefaction rarely spreads since tau_static is small). The free-field displacement is usually the input; pile pinning (MCEER/ATC-49; Boulanger et al., 2005) applied to approach embankments needs the embankment's finite out-of-plane width, and for interior bents in broad spreading no reduction occurs unless the upslope passive wedge extends beyond the spreading zone (Turner and Brandenberg, 2015). Peak inertial loads usually occur early and not with peak kinematic loads, which grow with accumulated displacement and vary with pore pressure (Brandenberg et al., 2007); Ashford et al. (2011) give validated reduction factors for concurrent inertia and the effect of liquefaction on spectral acceleration, and some DOTs specify 0.5 (Caltrans, 2013) or 0.25 (WASHDOT, 2015) on inertial loads; shaft force effects need not exceed column plastic hinging where columns are ductile elements. Foundation-only models miss the reversed load path in spreading, where foundation top movements load the columns, connections and superstructure: column demands go unrecognized (column failures and deck collapses are documented), and the beneficial redistribution of load through the superstructure to bents or abutments outside the spreading zone is lost (Cubrinovski et al., 2014; Turner et al., 2016; Franke and Rollins, 2017). Above-ground substructure must therefore be in the model, for example as illustrated in Figure 9-5 (as printed); if the software cannot do this, use another tool and/or work closely with the structural designer.
key_points: Lateral spreading (su,r > tau_static, needs inertia) vs flow slide (su,r < tau_static, usually needs ground improvement)
Equivalent-static: impose free-field displacement on p-y spring ends (Kavazanjian et al., 2011; Ashford et al., 2011)
With several feet of movement the crust passive load governs; design for it unless methods agree movement is minimal
Pile pinning only with finite embankment width or a passive wedge beyond the spread
Inertial reduction factors: Ashford et al. (2011); 0.5 Caltrans, 0.25 WSDOT; cap at column hinging
Model above-ground substructure: foundation-only models miss column demands and load sharing

sections.title: Cyclic Softening of Cohesive Soils
sections.body: [p. 9-51] Cohesive soils can lose strength under cyclic seismic loading, termed cyclic softening to distinguish it from liquefaction (Idriss and Boulanger, 2008); sensitive clays with low OCR are most susceptible. It can be modeled by a reduced su in the p-y curves, which changes both stiffness and ultimate resistance; 80 percent of the static su is a reasonable approximation. More explicit procedures (Idriss and Boulanger, 2008) range from index-property methods to cyclic laboratory tests on undisturbed samples, rarely warranted except for major structures in critical zones; the routine method computes the cohesive CRR for comparison with CSR, giving a factor of safety against cyclic softening alongside liquefaction analysis, as in commercial software.
key_points: Cyclic softening of sensitive, low-OCR clays
Use 80 percent of static su in p-y curves as a reasonable approximation
Routine method: CRR vs CSR for clays alongside liquefaction triggering

sections.title: Foundation Stiffness, Damping and Input Motions for Structural Analysis
sections.body: [pp. 9-51 to 9-52] Shaft supports are modeled either by a depth of fixity with columns fixed there, mainly to capture maximum moments and adequate for AASHTO (2017a) Seismic Zones 2 and 3 on site classes A to D, or by springs for each degree of freedom (misleadingly called soil springs, since they combine shaft and ground response), with lateral and rotational coefficients from p-y analysis and vertical from t-z analysis; elastic solutions are generally inadequate for layered, nonlinear, degrading profiles. Springs are strongly recommended in Zone 4 and for site classes E or F in Zones 2 and 3, and can be used anywhere (Kavazanjian et al., 2011). Structural software usually needs equivalent-linear spring constants, so structural and foundation designers must coordinate so springs match the force levels imposed. p-y software can generate stiffness matrices for given force effects; check compatibility and that each stiffness equals force divided by computed deformation. Cross-coupling (e.g., longitudinal moment also causing longitudinal displacement) can be significant and should be lumped with zero off-diagonal terms or entered explicitly if the program accepts full matrices. Equivalent-static and modal analyses need only stiffness; dynamic analyses may add damping by dashpots or percent of critical damping from simplified solutions (e.g., NIST 2012) or dynamic tests, e.g., Brown (2007) from rapid lateral load tests with a single degree of freedom model, or approximately by increasing p-y and t-z resistance: Paikowsky et al. (2004) found Statnamic rapid tests averaged 54% more resistance than static in clay, 45% in silt and 10% in sand, usable for preliminary design of layers without strength loss but to be verified by rapid load testing. Kinematic interaction also makes top-of-foundation motion differ from free-field motion, most for large shafts in soft near-surface soils (e.g., major estuarine crossings), often reducing the motion exciting the superstructure; hazard results exclude this, so input motions may be modified, e.g., by an effective support motion from free-field motion at depth (Kavazanjian et al., 2011) or the models of Turner et al. (2017).
key_points: Depth of fixity adequate in Zones 2 and 3 on site classes A to D; springs strongly recommended in Zone 4 and on E/F sites
Springs from p-y (lateral, rotational) and t-z (vertical); equivalent-linear at the expected force level
Check stiffness = force / deformation; handle cross-coupling
Damping by dashpots or percent critical; rapid tests: +54% clay, +45% silt, +10% sand (Paikowsky et al., 2004)
Kinematic interaction can reduce foundation input motion (Kavazanjian et al., 2011; Turner et al., 2017)
